464---
464+
465465 --  *Theorem*: Equivalence is a congruence for `while` -- that is, if `b`
466466 --  is equivalent to `b'` and `c` is equivalent to `c'`, then
467467 --  `while (~b) {~c}` is equivalent to `while (~b') {~c'}`.

477477 --    `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`. The only nontrivial cases are when
478478 --    the final rule in the derivation is `Com.EvalR.whileFalse` or
479479 --    `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`.

88 --  In an earlier chapter, we began applying the mathematical tools
99 --  developed in the first part of the course to studying the theory of a
1010 --  small programming language, Imp.
11---
11+
1212 --  - We defined a type of *abstract syntax trees* for Imp, together with
1313 --    an *evaluation relation* (a partial function on states) that
1414 --    specifies the *operational semantics* of programs.
15---
15+
1616 --    The language we defined, though small, captures some of the key
1717 --    features of full-blown languages like C, C++, and Java, including the
1818 --    fundamental notion of mutable state and some common control
1919 --    structures.
20---
20+
2121 --  - We proved a number of *metatheoretic properties* -- "meta" in the
2222 --    sense that they are properties of the language as a whole, rather
2323 --    than of particular programs in the language. These included:
24---
24+
2525 --    - determinism of evaluation
26---
26+
2727 --    - equivalence of some different ways of writing down the definitions
2828 --      (e.g., functional and relational definitions of arithmetic
2929 --      expression evaluation)
30---
30+
3131 --    - guaranteed termination of certain classes of programs
32---
32+
3333 --    - correctness (in the sense of preserving meaning) of a number of
3434 --      useful program transformations
35---
35+
3636 --    - behavioral equivalence of programs (in the Equiv chapter).
37---
37+
3838 --  If we stopped here, we would already have something useful: a set of
3939 --  tools for defining and discussing programming languages and language
4040 --  features that are mathematically precise, flexible, and easy to work
4545 --  not consciously recognize them as "theorems." But properties that seem
4646 --  intuitively obvious can sometimes be quite subtle (sometimes also
4747 --  subtly wrong!).
48---
48+

5050 --  theme of metatheoretic properties of whole languages when we discuss

5555 --  simple examples of *program verification* -- i.e., to use the precise
5656 --  definition of Imp to prove formally that particular programs satisfy
5757 --  particular specifications of their behavior.
58---

455457 --  ## Hoare Triples, Informally
457459 --  A *Hoare triple* is a claim about the state before and after executing
458460 --  a command. A commond notation for Hoare triples, and the one we use in
459461 --  this book, is
460---
461---      {{P}} c {{Q}}
462---
462+
463+--    {{P}} c {{Q}}
464+
463465 --  meaning:
464---
466+
465467 --  - If command `c` begins execution in a state satisfying assertion `P`,
466468 --  - and if `c` eventually terminates in some final state,
467469 --  - then that final state will satisfy the assertion `Q`.
468---
470+
469471 --  Assertion `P` is called the *precondition* of the triple, and `Q` is
470472 --  the *postcondition*.
471---
473+
472474 --  For example,
473---
475+
474476 --  - The Hoare triple
475---
476---      {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
477---
477+
478+--    {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
479+
478480 --  states that command `X := X + 1` will transform a state in which
479481 --  `X = 0` to a state in which `X = 1`.
480---
482+
481483 --  - On the other hand,
482---
483---      ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
484---
484+
485+--    ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
486+
485487 --  is a *proposition* stating that the Hoare triple
486488 --  `{{X = m}} X :=
487489 --  X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}` is valid for any choice of `m`.
488490 --  Note that `m` in the two assertions is a reference to the *Lean*
489491 --  variable `m`, which is bound outside the Hoare triple.

796778 --  The rule for assignment is the most fundamental of the Hoare logic
797779 --  proof rules. Here's how it works.
798---
780+
799781 --  Consider this incomplete Hoare triple:
800---
801---      {{ ??? }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
802---
782+
783+--    {{ ??? }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
784+
803785 --  We want to assign `Y` to `X` and finish in a state where `X` is `1`.
804786 --  What could the precondition be?
805---
787+
806788 --  One possibility is `Y = 1`, because if `Y` is already `1` then
807789 --  assigning it to `X` causes `X` to be `1`. That leads to a valid Hoare
808790 --  triple:
809---
810---      {{ Y = 1 }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
811---
791+
792+--    {{ Y = 1 }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
793+
812794 --  It may seem as though coming up with that precondition must have taken
813795 --  some clever thought. But there is a mechanical way we could have done
814796 --  it: if we take the postcondition `X = 1` and in it replace `X` with
816798 --  with the right-hand side---we get the precondition, `Y = 1`.
817799 
818800 --  That same idea works in more complicated cases. For example:
819---
820---      {{ ??? }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
821---
801+
802+--    {{ ??? }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
803+
822804 --  If we replace the `X` in `X = 1` with `X + Y`, we get `X + Y = 1`. That
823805 --  again leads to a valid Hoare triple:
824---
825---      {{ X + Y = 1 }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
826---
806+
807+--    {{ X + Y = 1 }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
808+
827809 --  Why does this technique work? The postcondition identifies some
828810 --  property `P` that we want to hold of the variable `X` being assigned.
829811 --  In this case, `P` is "equals `1`". To complete the triple and make it
836818 --  In general, the postcondition could be some arbitrary assertion `Q`,
837819 --  and the right-hand side of the assignment could be some arbitrary
838820 --  arithmetic expression `a`:
839---
840---      {{ ??? }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
841---
821+
822+--    {{ ??? }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
823+
842824 --  The precondition would then be `Q`, but with any occurrences of `X` in
843825 --  it replaced by `a`.
844---
826+
845827 --  Let's introduce a notation for this idea of replacing occurrences:
846828 --  Define `Q \[X ↦ a`] to mean "`Q` where `a` is substituted in place of
847829 --  `X`".

849831 --  This yields the Hoare logic rule for assignment:
850---
851---      {{ Q [X ↦ a] }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
852---
832+
833+--    {{ Q [X ↦ a] }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
834+
853835 --  One way of reading this rule is: If you want statement `X := a` to
854836 --  terminate in a state that satisfies assertion `Q`, then it suffices to
855837 --  start in a state that also satisfies `Q`, except where `a` is
860842 --  good sense to go in this direction: the postcondition is often what is
861843 --  more important, because it characterizes what will be true after
862844 --  running the code.
863---

864846 --  Nonetheless, it's also possible to formulate a "forward" assignment
865847 --  rule. We'll do that later in some exercises.

23332301 --  Our main task in this chapter has been to *define* the rules of Hoare
23342302 --  logic, and prove that the definitions are sound. Having done so, we can
23352303 --  go on and work *within* Hoare logic to prove that particular programs
23362304 --  satisfy particular Hoare triples. In the next chapter, we'll see how
23372305 --  Hoare logic is can be used to prove that more interesting programs
23382306 --  satisfy interesting specifications of their behavior.

23412309 --  of Hoare triples -- i.e., we will take the rules of Hoare logic as a
23422310 --  closed world for reasoning about programs.

6553 --  ## Decorated Programs
6654 
6755 --  The beauty of Hoare Logic is that it is *syntax directed*: the
6856 --  structure of proofs exactly follows the structure of programs.
69---
57+
7058 --  We can record the essential ideas of a Hoare-logic proof — omitting
7159 --  low-level calculational details — by "decorating" a program with
7260 --  appropriate assertions on each of its commands.
73---
61+
7462 --  Such a *decorated program* carries within itself an argument for its
7563 --  own correctness.
76---
64+
7765 --  For example, consider the program:
78---
79---      X := m;
80---      Z := p;
81---      while X <> 0 do
82---        Z := Z - 1;
83---        X := X - 1
84---      end
85---

68+--    Z := p;

70+--      Z := Z - 1;
71+--      X := X - 1
72+--    end

8674 --  Here is one possible specification for this program, in the form of a
8775 --  Hoare triple:
88---
89---      {{ True }}
90---      X := m;
91---      Z := p;
92---      while X <> 0 do
93---        Z := Z - 1;
94---        X := X - 1
95---      end
96---      {{ Z = p - m }}

83+--    end

106---        X := m
107---                           {{ X = m }} ->>

123111 --  Concretely, a decorated program consists of the program's text
124112 --  interleaved with assertions (sometimes multiple assertions separated by
125113 --  ->>).
126---
114+
127115 --  A decorated program can be viewed as a compact representation of a
128116 --  proof in Hoare Logic: the assertions surrounding each command specify
129117 --  the Hoare triple to be proved for that part of the program using one of
146134 --  Consider the following program, which swaps the values of two variables
147135 --  using addition and subtraction, instead of by assigning to a temporary
148136 --  variable.
149---
150---      X := X + Y;
151---      Y := X - Y;
152---      X := X - Y
153---
137+
138+--    X := X + Y;
139+--    Y := X - Y;
140+--    X := X - Y

154142 --  We can give a proof, in the form of decorations, that this program is
155143 --  correct — i.e., it really swaps `X` and `Y` — as follows.
156144 
157---      (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>
158---      (2)    {{ (X + Y) - ((X + Y) - Y) = n /\ (X + Y) - Y = m }}
159---               X := X + Y
160---      (3)                     {{ X - (X - Y) = n /\ X - Y = m }};
161---               Y := X - Y
162---      (4)                     {{ X - Y = n /\ Y = m }};
163---               X := X - Y
164---      (5)    {{ X = n /\ Y = m }}
165---
145+--    (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>
146+--    (2)    {{ (X + Y) - ((X + Y) - Y) = n /\ (X + Y) - Y = m }}
147+--             X := X + Y
148+--    (3)                     {{ X - (X - Y) = n /\ X - Y = m }};
149+--             Y := X - Y
150+--    (4)                     {{ X - Y = n /\ Y = m }};
151+--             X := X - Y
152+--    (5)    {{ X = n /\ Y = m }}
153+
166154 --  The decorations can be constructed as follows:
167---
155+
168156 --  - We begin with the undecorated program (the unnumbered lines).
169---
157+
170158 --  - We add the specification — i.e., the outer precondition (1) and
171159 --    postcondition (5). In the precondition, we use parameters `m` and `n`
172160 --    to remember the initial values of variables `X` and `Y` so that we
173161 --    can refer to them in the postcondition (5).
174---
162+
175163 --  - We work backwards, mechanically, starting from (5) and proceeding
176164 --    until we get to (2). At each step, we obtain the precondition of the
177165 --    assignment from its postcondition by substituting the assigned
178166 --    variable with the right-hand-side of the assignment. For instance, we
179167 --    obtain (4) by substituting `X` with `X - Y` in (5), and we obtain (3)
180168 --    by substituting `Y` with `X - Y` in (4).
181---
169+
182170 --  - Finally, we verify that (1) logically implies (2) — i.e., that the
183171 --    step from (1) to (2) is a valid use of the law of consequence — by
184172 --    doing a bit of high-school algebra.

199---                Z := X - Y
200---      (7)                    {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
201---              end
202---      (8)   {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}

189+--            end

298286 --  is divided by `n` and `Y` set to the quotient.

320---                Y := Y + 1

982972 --  creative part of a verifying program using Hoare Logic is finding the
983973 --  right loop invariants. The reason this is difficult is the same as the
984974 --  reason that inductive mathematical proofs are:
985---
975+
986976 --  - Strengthening a *loop invariant* means that you have a stronger
987977 --    assumption to work with when trying to establish the postcondition of
988978 --    the loop body, but it also means that the loop body's postcondition
989979 --    is harder to prove.
990---
980+
991981 --  - Similarly, strengthening an *induction hypothesis* means that you
992982 --    have a stronger assumption to work with when trying to complete the
993983 --    induction step of the proof, but it also means that the statement
994984 --    being proved inductively is harder to prove.
995---
985+

997987 --  invariants through a series of examples and exercises.

10331023 --  Examining this skeleton, we can see that any valid `Inv` will have to
10341024 --  respect three conditions:
1035---

10361026 --  - (a) it must be *weak* enough to be implied by the loop's
10371027 --    precondition, i.e., (1) must imply (2);

10401030 --    i.e., (7) must imply (8);

10431033 --    assuming that the loop guard also evaluates to true, i.e., (3) must
10441034 --    imply (4).
10461036 --  These conditions are actually independent of the particular program and
10471037 --  specification we are considering: every loop invariant has to satisfy
10481038 --  them.

10521042 --  "candidate" invariant (e.g., a guess or a heuristic choice) and check
10531043 --  the three conditions above; if any of the checks fails, try to use the
10541044 --  information that we get from the failure to produce another — hopefully
10551045 --  better — candidate invariant, and repeat.

2424 --  We concentrate here on defining the *syntax* and *semantics* of Imp;
2525 --  later in this volume we develop a theory of *program equivalence* and
3434 --  *relation* (proved equivalent), and a small `optimize0plus` program
3535 --  transformation together with its correctness proof. Those expressions
3636 --  are *variable-free*.

3838 --  This chapter picks up from there. First we extend the expressions with
3939 --  *variables*; then we add a language of *commands* — assignment,
4040 --  conditionals, sequencing, and loops.

109109 --  Briefly, though, here is how the two blocks below fit together:

113113 --    further below.

13121339 --  appropriately:

13341361 --    propagate the signal generated there.
